A commenter first thought Crossplane was 'a bunch of presets operating on k8s' and disliked the idea of DBs running inside the cluster rather than on RDS/CloudSQL. After reading the design doc they called it 'very clever': cloud-agnostic custom resources plus cloud-specific controllers. Their caveat was that you must set up your own k8s manually, with no way to bootstrap.

Compared to the AWS Service Operator, Crossplane works like Kubernetes Persistent Volumes: apps request an abstract class and the cluster owner maps it to concrete cloud resources. Using AWS operator APIs directly in a Helm chart ties the app to AWS, while this abstraction enables portability to databases, serverless and other services.

The AWS operator only targets AWS resources, so you can't take them to minikube, Azure or elsewhere. Some would call that a form of vendor lock-in. Crossplane is about using services with apps that stay portable across cloud providers.

On Crossplane vs Terraform: you would likely use both. Terraform provisions the Kubernetes cluster and non-app infrastructure. Crossplane puts app-specific infra (e.g. a MySQL DB) in the same config as the Kubernetes app, so you don't have to pre-provision with Terraform and keep it in sync.

GitLab is excited about Crossplane as the missing piece for convenient multi-cloud. Its Helm chart doesn't set up object storage or managed PostgreSQL/Redis, so GitLab plans to deploy that way first and then integrate Crossplane into Auto DevOps for app portability.

Skeptical take: 'While i really like the idea, i'm looking forward to see if we moved our problems down to the operator code or if those configuration problems are gone.' The commenter also asked why you must configure a MySQL DB for WordPress when it always needs one.

A commenter likes separating a service's infra requirements from its implementation details. They doubted the 'separation of concerns between developers and administrators' pitch, asking how it works where developers administer their own services.

Feedback on communication: the launch blog didn't link back to the product site, leaving readers wondering what the product is. Another user said a maintainer's HN comment 'did a better job explaining your product than the website.'

A user wouldn't trust AWS/Google to host Crossplane with equal footing for competitors, so a vendor-neutral company model may work. They also noted that 'Crossplane' and 'Upbound' seem too unrelated as names.
A self-described 'frustrated cloud user' welcomed Crossplane and said they would support it 'if you guys stay true to your mission.'

Asked whether Crossplane competes with Rancher 2.0, one user said it complements it. You'd run Crossplane on a Rancher cluster to get automatically provisioned databases, since it extends the default kube system.

A user has often seen Terraform fall apart for large teams. They resort to ever-smaller modules (less drift blast radius, less visibility) or '-target' applies. Crossplane appears to have clear YAML that's easy to commit to source control, and its control plane for enforcement seems easier than setting up Atlantis.

Many teams run GitOps with Flux/ArgoCD for k8s apps but can't fit Terraform into that workflow. The commenter is interested in Crossplane for a single GitOps flow where app teams self-service infra from the app cluster alongside their Deployments.
